l: Colonos, The Seven Plays in English Verse, _Enter_ THESEUS.
s: Colonos is identified as the deme whose god-protected sacred place has received Oedipus as a suppliant. Creon's removal of the children from this refuge is condemned as an unlicensed inroad against an ancient city.

l: Creon's capture of Oedipus's children, The Seven Plays in English Verse, _Enter_ THESEUS.
s: Creon's capture of Oedipus's children is treated by Theseus as an unlawful seizure of suppliants that disgraces Creon, Thebes, and Colonos. Theseus sends forces to intercept the captors and orders Creon to help recover the children.

l: parricide, The Seven Plays in English Verse, _Enter_ THESEUS.
s: Creon identifies Oedipus's crimes as parricide, incest, and the defilement of his mother's bed. Oedipus answers that he committed these acts unknowingly, fulfilling a divine oracle and acting without knowledge of his father's or mother's identity.

l: The Seven Plays in English Verse, The Seven Plays in English Verse, CHORUS.
s: Theseus returns Oedipus's daughters safely after rescuing them, and Oedipus praises him and Athens for their justice and protection. Polynices comes as a suppliant, asking Oedipus to support his campaign against Thebes, but Oedipus curses him and Eteocles, declaring that they will die by one another's hands. Antigone urges Polynices to abandon the war because the prophecy foretells mutual death, but he refuses and departs to face his doomed enterprise. The Chorus celebrates the rescue, anticipates battle, and reflects that death is the final release from life's suffering.

l: Oedipus, The Seven Plays in English Verse, CHORUS.
s: Oedipus rejoices when Theseus brings Antigone and her sister back safely, and he credits Theseus alone with saving them. He permits Polynices to speak, but condemns him for having driven him into exile and declares that his curse will defeat Polynices's attempt against Thebes.

l: Theseus, The Seven Plays in English Verse, CHORUS.
s: Theseus returns with Oedipus's daughters unharmed after protecting them from their captors. He brings Polynices from Poseidon's altar under safe-conduct and assures Oedipus that no one will interfere with his freedom.

l: Antigone, The Seven Plays in English Verse, CHORUS.
s: Antigone rejoices at her rescue and asks Oedipus to hear Polynices, persuading him to yield to Theseus's request. She urges Polynices to turn back his army because their father's prophecy foretells that he and Eteocles will kill each other, but he refuses and leaves.

l: Ismene, The Seven Plays in English Verse, CHORUS.
s: Ismene is present with Antigone when Theseus returns them safely to Oedipus, but she has no individual speech in this unit.

l: Polynices, The Seven Plays in English Verse, CHORUS.
s: Polynices comes as a suppliant to ask Oedipus's aid for his campaign to recover his throne from Eteocles. Oedipus rejects him and curses his attempt, predicting that Polynices will die by a fratricidal hand and kill the brother who banished him. Polynices accepts that he is heading toward death, refuses Antigone's plea to withdraw, and departs.

l: Eteocles, The Seven Plays in English Verse, CHORUS.
s: Eteocles is said to have exiled Polynices and taken the throne through the people's support after Polynices claimed the right to rule. Oedipus includes him in the curse that predicts fraternal death.

l: Chorus of Village Guardians, The Seven Plays in English Verse, CHORUS.
s: The Chorus anticipates a battle between the forces of Theseus and the opposing army, praises Athena's champions, and celebrates the return of Oedipus's daughters. It later reflects that prolonged life brings suffering and that death ultimately ends the struggle, then pities Polynices after Oedipus curses him.

l: Argive army, The Seven Plays in English Verse, CHORUS.
s: Polynices says that his army consists of seven battalions led by prominent warriors, including Amphiaráus, Tydeus, Etéoclus, Hippomedon, Capaneus, Parthenopaeus, and himself. The army surrounds the plain of Thebes to support Polynices's attempt to regain power.

l: Athens, The Seven Plays in English Verse, CHORUS.
s: Oedipus praises Athens as the one place where he has found piety, justice, and truth in word and deed. Its ruler Theseus protects Oedipus and his daughters and guarantees safe conduct for Polynices.

l: Thebes, The Seven Plays in English Verse, CHORUS.
s: Thebes is the land from which Polynices was exiled and where Eteocles now holds power. Polynices's army is gathered against Thebes, while Antigone warns that the campaign will bring ruin to the city as well as to Polynices.

l: Argos, The Seven Plays in English Verse, CHORUS.
s: Polynices says that he went to Argos, married Adrastus's child, and raised a friendly army there. He intends to return from Argos after defeating those who hold Theban power.

l: the conflict between Eteocles and Polynices, The Seven Plays in English Verse, CHORUS.
s: The Chorus expects a battle between the forces associated with Theseus and their foes, but no battle is shown in this unit. Polynices's coming battle against Thebes is presented as an enterprise already doomed by Oedipus's prophecy and curse.

l: the attack on Thebes, The Seven Plays in English Verse, CHORUS.
s: Polynices leads seven commanders and their forces against Thebes to recover the throne from Eteocles. Antigone urges him to abandon the campaign, but he insists that withdrawing would be shameful and departs to continue it.

l: Oedipus's curse, The Seven Plays in English Verse, CHORUS.
s: Oedipus renews his curse against Polynices and Eteocles, calling on Zeus, Justice, and the powers of the underworld. He declares that Polynices will fail to return to Argos, will die by a fratricidal hand, and will kill the brother who banished him.

l: the deaths of Polynices and Eteocles, The Seven Plays in English Verse, CHORUS.
s: Oedipus prophesies that Polynices and Eteocles will kill one another. Antigone recognizes the prophecy as a warning against the war, but Polynices dismisses the danger and proceeds.

l: death, The Seven Plays in English Verse, CHORUS.
s: The Chorus describes death as the final release from the bitterness and weariness of life, calling it a dark bridegroom without celebration. Polynices accepts that he may die and leaves to meet the fate foretold by Oedipus.

l: The Seven Plays in English Verse, The Seven Plays in English Verse, CHORUS.
s: Oedipus recognizes that the Gods' thunder and lightning announce his imminent death and asks Theseus to come. He leads Theseus and his daughters to the sacred place where he is to die, entrusting Theseus with a secret that will protect Athens and asking him to safeguard Antigone and Ismene. Oedipus disappears from the sight of his companions in a mysterious, painless manner, leaving Theseus as the only witness. Antigone and Ismene mourn him and ask Theseus to help them return to Thebes, which he promises to do.

l: Oedipus, The Seven Plays in English Verse, CHORUS.
s: Oedipus understands the thunder and lightning as signs that his divinely promised death is near. He leads his daughters to his appointed resting-place, entrusts Theseus with a secret meant to protect Athens, and disappears mysteriously after asking Theseus to protect Antigone and Ismene.

l: Antigone, The Seven Plays in English Verse, CHORUS.
s: Antigone remains with Oedipus during his final moments and questions him about the signs of his approaching death. After his disappearance, she mourns him intensely and asks Theseus to let her see his resting-place and to provide an escort back to Thebes.

l: Ismene, The Seven Plays in English Verse, CHORUS.
s: Ismene helps prepare Oedipus by bringing water with Antigone and shares in the farewell. She grieves after his disappearance, longs for death with her honored father, and asks where she and Antigone can find refuge before Theseus promises to aid them.

l: Theseus, The Seven Plays in English Verse, CHORUS.
s: Theseus comes in response to the thunder and Oedipus's summons. He swears to protect Antigone and Ismene, keeps Oedipus's resting-place secret, and refuses their request to approach it, but promises to escort them back to Thebes.

l: the Chorus, The Seven Plays in English Verse, CHORUS.
s: The Chorus interprets the thunder and lightning as divine signs and prays to Zeus and the powers of the Underworld for Oedipus's peaceful passage. After his disappearance, it urges Antigone and Ismene to stop mourning and assures them that they are protected in Athens.

l: the Gods, The Seven Plays in English Verse, CHORUS.
s: The Gods announce Oedipus's appointed end through thunder, lightning, and divine voices. Hermes and the Queen of realms below are said to guide him, and a divine summons calls him onward before he disappears.

l: Athens, The Seven Plays in English Verse, CHORUS.
s: Athens is promised protection through the secret connected with Oedipus's resting-place, provided that Theseus keeps the secret faithfully. Theseus also promises to support Oedipus's daughters and help them return to Thebes.

l: the blind stranger's death, The Seven Plays in English Verse, CHORUS.
s: The blind stranger's death is described as peaceful, mysterious, and free from sickness, war, or violence. He is taken from the Earth without a visible grave or ordinary burial, and the Chorus calls his end fortunate.

l: Oedipus's disappearance, The Seven Plays in English Verse, CHORUS.
s: Oedipus disappears after dismissing his daughters and remaining alone with Theseus. No lightning-flash or tempest causes it; the Messenger says that a heavenly messenger or the Earth opening beneath him may have carried him away, and that only Theseus witnessed what happened.

l: Oedipus's resting-place, The Seven Plays in English Verse, CHORUS.
s: Oedipus's resting-place is a sacred and secret spot near the stone basin and the landmarks described by the Messenger. No one may approach or speak of its location, because Oedipus has promised that its secret will help keep Athens safe from its enemies.

l: The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, HECUBA.
s: The Ghost of Polydore explains that Priam secretly sent him, with gold, to Polymestor in Thrace for protection, but Polymestor murdered him for the gold and cast his body into the sea. Achilles has appeared above his tomb and demanded Polyxena as a sacrifice, so the Greeks will take her from Hecuba. Polydore’s body is being carried by the waves toward the shore, where Hecuba will see it along with Polyxena’s corpse. Hecuba, once a queen of Troy, is now enslaved and suffers the destruction of her family and city.

l: Hecuba, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, HECUBA.
s: Hecuba is the daughter of Cisseus, the mother of Polydore and Polyxena, and the former queen of Troy. She is now enslaved and held in the Chersonese near Agamemnon’s tent. She is advancing from the tent, and Polydore foresees that she will see the corpses of both her children.

l: Polydore, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, HECUBA.
s: Polydore is the youngest son of Priam and Hecuba. Priam secretly sent him with gold to Polymestor for protection, but Polymestor murdered him for the gold and threw his body into the sea. His body is being carried onto the shore, where he hopes to receive burial and fall into Hecuba’s hands.

l: Ghost of Polydore, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, HECUBA.
s: The Ghost of Polydore has left the realm of the dead to describe his murder and the fate awaiting his family. He says that he will withdraw as Hecuba approaches and that he will appear on a wave before a female slave so that he may be buried.

l: Polyxena, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, HECUBA.
s: Polyxena is Hecuba’s daughter and Polydore’s sister. Achilles has demanded her as a victim, and the Greeks will take her to be sacrificed as an honor to Achilles’ tomb.

l: Priam, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, HECUBA.
s: Priam was Polydore’s father. Fearing the fall of Troy, he secretly sent Polydore to Polymestor with a large quantity of gold so that his surviving children would have support if the city fell. Priam was later slain at an altar by the blood-polluted son of Achilles.

l: Polymestor, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, HECUBA.
s: Polymestor is the Thracian friend of Priam and ruler of a warlike people in the Chersonese. Although he had received Polydore into his care, he murdered him to seize the gold and threw his body into the sea.

l: Achilles, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, HECUBA.
s: Achilles appears above his tomb after the Greeks are preparing to depart. He demands Polyxena as a sacrificial victim and tribute of honor to his tomb.

l: Hector, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, HECUBA.
s: Hector was Polydore’s brother and fought successfully with his spear while Troy’s landmarks and towers remained standing. His death accompanied the destruction of Troy.

l: Greeks, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, HECUBA.
s: The Greeks captured Troy and are holding their ships along the shores of the Chersonese. Achilles’ appearance stops them from departing, and they agree to give Polyxena as a sacrifice.

l: Troy, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, HECUBA.
s: Troy is the city of the Phrygians and the home of Priam’s family. Its walls and towers fell, its mansions were destroyed, and its capture left Hecuba and the other women enslaved.

l: Thracian Chersonese, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, HECUBA.
s: The Chersonese is the Thracian land where the Greeks have anchored after the capture of Troy. Polymestor rules part of it, and Hecuba and the captive women are held there near the Greek tents.

l: Polydore's gold, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, HECUBA.
s: Priam sent a large quantity of gold with Polydore so that his surviving children would have support if Troy fell. Polymestor murdered Polydore in order to possess the gold.

l: tomb of Achilles, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, HECUBA.
s: Achilles appears above his tomb and demands that Polyxena be given as a victim and tribute of honor. The Greeks stop their departure in response to this demand.

l: fall of Troy, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, HECUBA.
s: The capture of Troy leads to the destruction of the city, the death of Priam and Hector, and the enslavement of Hecuba and the other women. It also causes Polymestor to murder Polydore in order to take the gold.

l: sacrifice of Polyxena, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, HECUBA.
s: Achilles demands the sacrifice of Polyxena after appearing above his tomb. The Greeks will take her from Hecuba and offer her as an honor to Achilles.

l: murder of Polydore, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, HECUBA.
s: Polymestor murders Polydore, despite having received him from Priam as a charge to protect. He kills him for the gold and casts his body into the sea.

l: fall of Troy, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, HECUBA.
s: The fall of Troy brings about the destruction of its walls, towers, and royal mansions. Priam and Hector die, Hecuba becomes enslaved, and Polydore’s protection in Thrace is no longer secure.

l: Hecuba's revenge, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, HECUBA.
s: This unit does not describe Hecuba’s revenge, but the argument states that she will later kill Polymestor’s sons and blind Polymestor after luring him to her.

l: burial of Polydore, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, HECUBA.
s: Polydore’s body is unwept and unburied after being cast into the sea. He says that he has entreated the powers beneath to obtain a tomb and hopes that his body will reach Hecuba so that he can receive burial.

l: The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, HECUBA. CHORUS.
s: Hecuba learns that the Greeks have decreed the sacrifice of her daughter Polyxena at Achilles's tomb. Ulysses arrives to take Polyxena away, while Hecuba appeals to him by recalling that she once saved his life. Polyxena accepts death rather than slavery and indignity, and she is led away despite Hecuba's grief. The Chorus laments its enslavement and the destruction of Troy, wondering where the Trojan women will be taken.

l: Hecuba, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, HECUBA. CHORUS.
s: Hecuba is warned that Polyxena will be sacrificed at Achilles's tomb. She unsuccessfully begs Ulysses to spare her daughter, offers herself in Polyxena's place, and grieves over the loss of her children, city, and royal position.

l: Polyxena, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, HECUBA. CHORUS.
s: Polyxena learns that the Greek army has voted for her death. She refuses to plead for life, choosing death over enslavement and possible abuse, and bids farewell to Hecuba before being led away.

l: Ulysses, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, HECUBA. CHORUS.
s: Ulysses comes to conduct Polyxena to the sacrifice. He acknowledges that Hecuba once saved him when he was a spy in Troy, but says that Achilles must be honored and refuses to release Polyxena.

l: Achilles, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, HECUBA. CHORUS.
s: Achilles is regarded by the Greeks as the noblest and most glorious of their dead warriors. His tomb is said to demand a Trojan woman as a sacrificial honor.

l: Agamemnon, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, HECUBA. CHORUS.
s: Agamemnon initially supports Hecuba's interest and opposes sacrificing Polyxena, partly because he loves Cassandra.

l: Chorus, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, HECUBA. CHORUS.
s: The Chorus, composed of captive Trojan women, brings Hecuba the news of the Greek decision. It laments slavery, the destruction of Troy, Polyxena's fate, and its own uncertain future among foreign masters.

l: Trojan women, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, HECUBA. CHORUS.
s: The Trojan women have been allotted as slaves and led captive by the Greeks after Troy's fall. They are associated with the Chorus and face separation, forced labor, and uncertain destinations.

l: Greeks, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, HECUBA. CHORUS.
s: The Greeks debate whether Achilles's tomb should receive a victim and finally decree Polyxena's sacrifice. They justify the decision as honoring a warrior who died for Greece and maintaining honor for the brave dead.

l: Trojans, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, HECUBA. CHORUS.
s: The Trojans have lost their city and royal family, and their surviving women have been captured and enslaved by the Greeks.

l: Troy, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, HECUBA. CHORUS.
s: Troy has been captured and overthrown by the Argive sword, with its destruction described as buried in smoke.

l: Thrace, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, HECUBA. CHORUS.
s: Thrace is where Hecuba's only surviving son, Polydore, is believed to live under the protection of his father's friend. Hecuba fears for him because of her troubling dream.

l: tomb of Achilles, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, HECUBA. CHORUS.
s: Achilles's tomb is the place designated for Polyxena's sacrifice. Achilles's apparition appears above it and demands the honor of a Trojan victim.

l: Greek army's decree, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, HECUBA. CHORUS.
s: The Greek army's decree orders that Polyxena be offered at Achilles's tomb and appoints the son of Achilles to preside over the rites. Ulysses is ordered to conduct her there.

l: sacrifice of Polyxena, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, HECUBA. CHORUS.
s: The sacrifice of Polyxena is approved by the Greeks after debate. Polyxena accepts it and is taken away to die by the sword or pyre of Achilles.

l: fall of Troy, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, HECUBA. CHORUS.
s: The fall of Troy has made Hecuba a slave and deprived her of her husband, children, city, and royal status. The Chorus likewise describes Asia as conquered and its people as transferred into slavery in Europe.

l: Achilles's apparition, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, HECUBA. CHORUS.
s: Achilles's apparition appears above his tomb in golden armor while the Greek fleet is preparing to depart. It demands that the Greeks honor his tomb with a sacrifice.

l: Hecuba's dream, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, HECUBA. CHORUS.
s: Hecuba dreams of a dappled hind being torn from her bosom by a blood-stained wolf and sees Achilles's specter demanding a Trojan woman. She fears that the dream concerns Polyxena and possibly her son in Thrace.

l: slavery, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, HECUBA. CHORUS.
s: Slavery is presented as the fate of the captured Trojan women, who may be purchased, forced to labor, and subjected to masters' sexual power. Hecuba and the Chorus describe slavery as degrading and unbearable.

l: death, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, HECUBA. CHORUS.
s: Polyxena considers death preferable to living as a slave without honor. Hecuba begs to die with her daughter, but Ulysses says that Polyxena's death alone is required.

l: honor for the dead, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, HECUBA. CHORUS.
s: The Greeks argue that Achilles must receive honor after death because he died gloriously for Greece. Ulysses claims that failing to honor him would discourage future warriors and bring disgrace on the army.

l: Hecuba's children, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, HECUBA. CHORUS.
s: Hecuba has lost many children, including Hector and other sons, and says that only Polyxena has remained as her consolation. She also fears for Polydore, her son living in Thrace.

l: Trojan royal house, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, HECUBA. CHORUS.
s: The Trojan royal house has been destroyed: Hecuba's husband and children are gone, and she has become a slave. Polyxena recalls that she was once the daughter of a king and expected to marry a prince.

l: The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, TALTHYBIUS, HECUBA, CHORUS.
s: Talthybius tells Hecuba how Polyxena was sacrificed at Achilles' tomb by the Greeks, describing her courage, dignity, and death. Hecuba, now a captive and bereft of her children, mourns Polyxena and asks to prepare her body for burial. The Chorus attributes Troy's destruction to the judgment of Paris and the war that followed Helen's abduction. The unit contrasts Hecuba's former royal prosperity with her present misery and reflects on the instability of human fortune.

l: Talthybius, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, TALTHYBIUS, HECUBA, CHORUS.
s: Talthybius, the herald of the Greeks, is sent by Agamemnon to Hecuba. He reports Polyxena's sacrifice in detail and describes the pity and admiration her death aroused among the Greeks.

l: Hecuba, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, TALTHYBIUS, HECUBA, CHORUS.
s: Hecuba lies on the ground as an aged, captive, childless former queen. After hearing of Polyxena's death, she mourns her daughter, asks that the Greeks protect the body, and prepares to wash and adorn it.

l: Trojan women, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, TALTHYBIUS, HECUBA, CHORUS.
s: The Trojan women identify where Hecuba is lying and witness her grief. They are captives living in tents under the authority of their new lords.

l: Chorus, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, TALTHYBIUS, HECUBA, CHORUS.
s: The Chorus laments the calamities that have overtaken Priam's house and attributes them to the harsh fate of the Gods. It recalls the judgment on Ida, the war, the destruction of Troy, and the grief of Trojan and Spartan women.

l: Troy, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, TALTHYBIUS, HECUBA, CHORUS.
s: Troy has been overthrown by the spear, and its former royal household has been reduced to captivity and misery. Its destruction is linked to Paris's decision and the war over Helen.

l: Priam, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, TALTHYBIUS, HECUBA, CHORUS.
s: Priam is remembered as the wealthy and supremely blessed king of Troy, possessing a great household and many children. Hecuba now laments the loss of his former prosperity.

l: Greeks, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, TALTHYBIUS, HECUBA, CHORUS.
s: The Greeks sacrifice Polyxena at the tomb of Achilles and later honor her body with leaves and funeral offerings. Their army is portrayed as capable of disorder and harshness, though it also responds to Polyxena's courage and grants her request to die freely.

l: Polyxena, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, TALTHYBIUS, HECUBA, CHORUS.
s: Polyxena is taken to Achilles' tomb and faces death with courage and dignity. She refuses to be restrained, asks to die free, exposes her neck or breast to the sword, and maintains modesty even as she dies.

l: Agamemnon, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, TALTHYBIUS, HECUBA, CHORUS.
s: Agamemnon sends Talthybius to Hecuba. At Polyxena's sacrifice, he orders the young men to release her after the army assents to her request.

l: Neoptolemus, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, TALTHYBIUS, HECUBA, CHORUS.
s: The son of Achilles leads Polyxena to the summit of the mound, pours libations to his dead father, and calls for the sacrifice. He kills Polyxena with his sword, showing pity while carrying out the act, and directs that her body be honored.

l: Greek army, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, TALTHYBIUS, HECUBA, CHORUS.
s: The Greek army gathers at Achilles' tomb for Polyxena's sacrifice, joins in prayer, and observes silence during the ritual. After her death, its members scatter leaves and gather materials for her funeral, while some are rebuked for failing to bring offerings.

l: sacrifice of Polyxena, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, TALTHYBIUS, HECUBA, CHORUS.
s: Polyxena is sacrificed at Achilles' tomb so that the Greeks may gain a prosperous return from Troy. She dies willingly and nobly, asking to remain free in death; afterward, the Greeks prepare funeral honors for her.

l: Hecuba's enslavement and fall, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, TALTHYBIUS, HECUBA, CHORUS.
s: Hecuba has fallen from being queen of the wealthy Phrygians and wife of Priam to being an aged captive lying in the dust. She is childless after Polyxena's death and reflects that human prosperity can vanish completely.

l: the Trojan War, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, TALTHYBIUS, HECUBA, CHORUS.
s: The Trojan War has brought slaughter, the desolation of palaces, the destruction of Troy, and the enslavement of its women. The Chorus presents the war as a public calamity arising from Paris's decision concerning the three Goddesses and Helen.

l: Paris, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, TALTHYBIUS, HECUBA, CHORUS.
s: Paris is described as hewing pine on Ida and preparing to cross the sea to Helen. The Chorus treats his action and the choice associated with him as the source of a calamity fatal to Troy.

l: Helen, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, TALTHYBIUS, HECUBA, CHORUS.
s: Helen is called the fairest woman illuminated by the sun's golden beams. Her relationship with Paris is presented as the cause of the conflict that brought suffering to Troy and Greece.

l: the judgment of Paris, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, TALTHYBIUS, HECUBA, CHORUS.
s: The judgment of Paris is recalled as a dispute among the three daughters of the Gods on Ida. The decision is associated with war, slaughter, the destruction of Troy's palaces, and widespread mourning.

l: Hecuba's household, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, TALTHYBIUS, HECUBA, CHORUS.
s: Hecuba's household, once associated with Priam's wealth, royal mansions, and many children, has been reduced to nothing. Its members have been killed, enslaved, or otherwise separated, leaving Hecuba to mourn its lost grandeur.

l: The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, FEMALE ATTENDANT, CHORUS, HECUBA.
s: Hecuba learns that her son Polydore has been murdered by Polymestor, who cast his body into the sea, after Polyxena was sacrificed by the Greeks. She appeals to Agamemnon to punish Polymestor, invoking hospitality, the gods, and justice. Agamemnon agrees to help if he can avoid opposition from the Greek army, and Hecuba plans to use the captive Trojan women to take revenge. The Chorus mourns the destruction of Troy and the enslavement and exile of its women.

l: Hecuba, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, FEMALE ATTENDANT, CHORUS, HECUBA.
s: Hecuba receives the corse of her son Polydore and recognizes that Polymestor has murdered him for his gold. She appeals to Agamemnon for justice and permission to avenge the murder, and plans to use the captive Trojan women in her revenge.

l: Chorus, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, FEMALE ATTENDANT, CHORUS, HECUBA.
s: The Chorus witnesses Hecuba's grief, mourns the successive deaths of Polyxena and Polydore, and comments on the changes wrought by fortune and law. It laments the destruction of Troy, the deaths of its men, and the captivity and exile of the Trojan women.

l: Agamemnon, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, FEMALE ATTENDANT, CHORUS, HECUBA.
s: Agamemnon comes to ensure that Polyxena is buried and hears Hecuba's accusation against Polymestor. He agrees to assist her revenge if he can avoid appearing to act against the king of Thrace for Cassandra's sake, and he agrees to delay Polyxena's tomb until Polydore and Polyxena can be buried together.

l: Polyxena, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, FEMALE ATTENDANT, CHORUS, HECUBA.
s: Polyxena has been sacrificed by the Greeks, and Hecuba is expected to bury her. Agamemnon agrees to delay the raising of her tomb so that her ashes can be interred beside those of Polydore.

l: Polydore, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, FEMALE ATTENDANT, CHORUS, HECUBA.
s: Polydore was sent away from Troy by his father for protection and was placed with Polymestor, who was entrusted with his safety and with gold. Polymestor murdered him after learning of Troy's fall and cast his mutilated body into the sea.

l: Polymestor, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, FEMALE ATTENDANT, CHORUS, HECUBA.
s: Polymestor, king of the Thracians, was the guardian of Polydore and his gold. He murdered Polydore for the gold, despite having shared hospitality with Hecuba, and failed to provide the body with a tomb.

l: Greeks, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, FEMALE ATTENDANT, CHORUS, HECUBA.
s: The Greeks destroyed Troy and sacrificed Polyxena. Their army regards Polymestor as a friend and Polydore as an enemy, so Agamemnon fears that helping Hecuba may provoke opposition.

l: Thracians, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, FEMALE ATTENDANT, CHORUS, HECUBA.
s: The Thracians include the host to which Polymestor belongs. Hecuba asks that Polymestor and his sons be summoned to hear her words.

l: Troy, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, FEMALE ATTENDANT, CHORUS, HECUBA.
s: Troy has been destroyed by the Greeks, its men killed, and its women taken captive. The Chorus describes its towers as broken, its streets as filled with slaughter, and its buildings as darkened by smoke.

l: Thrace, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, FEMALE ATTENDANT, CHORUS, HECUBA.
s: Thrace is the country where Polydore was sent for concealment and where Polymestor rules. Hecuba identifies Polymestor as the man who murdered Polydore there.

l: Polydore's corse, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, FEMALE ATTENDANT, CHORUS, HECUBA.
s: Polydore's corse is found naked on the wave-washed shore after being cast up by the sea. Its wounds reveal that the boy was murdered, and Hecuba asks Agamemnon to help avenge the deed.

l: fall of Troy, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, FEMALE ATTENDANT, CHORUS, HECUBA.
s: The fall of Troy leads Polymestor to believe that he can seize Polydore's gold without consequence. It also results in the deaths of Trojan men, the sacrifice of Polyxena, and the enslavement and exile of the Trojan women.

l: sacrifice of Polyxena, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, FEMALE ATTENDANT, CHORUS, HECUBA.
s: Polyxena has been sacrificed, and Talthybius has reported that the Greeks will not prevent her burial. Agamemnon orders that her tomb's construction be delayed so that she can be buried beside Polydore.

l: murder of Polydore, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, FEMALE ATTENDANT, CHORUS, HECUBA.
s: Polymestor murders Polydore for the gold entrusted to him and casts the mutilated body into the sea without a tomb. Hecuba calls the act impious and asks Agamemnon to punish its perpetrator.

l: Hecuba's revenge, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, FEMALE ATTENDANT, CHORUS, HECUBA.
s: Hecuba plans to avenge Polydore with the captive Trojan women. Agamemnon consents to assist or suppress opposition, provided that his actions do not appear to be a private attack on the Thracian king.

l: hospitality and its laws, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, FEMALE ATTENDANT, CHORUS, HECUBA.
s: Hecuba argues that Polymestor violated the laws of hospitality by murdering a guest and former friend after sharing her table and receiving what was due for his services. She maintains that neither the gods nor the sacred laws can be honored if such a crime goes unpunished.

l: Justice, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, FEMALE ATTENDANT, CHORUS, HECUBA.
s: Hecuba appeals to the gods, law, and Agamemnon's sense of justice against Polymestor. Agamemnon agrees that the wicked should suffer vengeance and that Hecuba may seek punishment for the murder.

l: slavery, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, FEMALE ATTENDANT, CHORUS, HECUBA.
s: Hecuba describes herself as once a queen but now a slave, childless, cityless, and captive. The Chorus describes the Trojan women as dragged from their city and carried across the sea into captivity.

l: The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, POLYMESTOR, HECUBA, CHORUS.
s: Hecuba lures Polymestor into the tents by claiming that Polydore's gold and other treasures are hidden there. Hecuba and the Trojan women kill Polymestor's children and blind Polymestor in revenge for his murder of Polydore. Before Agamemnon, Polymestor claims that he killed Polydore to protect the Greeks and Thrace, while Hecuba argues that greed caused the murder. Agamemnon judges Polymestor guilty and orders him removed, while the Greeks prepare to sail from Troy.

l: Hecuba, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, POLYMESTOR, HECUBA, CHORUS.
s: Hecuba lures Polymestor into the tents by claiming that treasures, including Polydore's gold, are hidden there. With the Trojan women, she kills Polymestor's children and blinds Polymestor, avenging Polydore's murder. Before Agamemnon, she argues that Polymestor killed Polydore for the gold.

l: Polymestor, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, POLYMESTOR, HECUBA, CHORUS.
s: Polymestor says that Polydore is alive and well, but he later admits that he killed him. Hecuba and the Trojan women kill his children and blind him, after which he pursues them helplessly and appeals to Agamemnon. Agamemnon judges him guilty and orders him cast out on a desert island.

l: Agamemnon, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, POLYMESTOR, HECUBA, CHORUS.
s: Agamemnon comes after hearing Polymestor's cries and listens to both Polymestor and Hecuba. He decides that Polymestor killed his guest for the gold rather than for the benefit of the Greeks, and he orders Polymestor removed.

l: Polydore, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, POLYMESTOR, HECUBA, CHORUS.
s: Polydore is identified as the youngest of Priam's children and Hecuba's son. Priam sent him to Polymestor for protection and upbringing, but Polymestor killed him.

l: Chorus, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, POLYMESTOR, HECUBA, CHORUS.
s: The Chorus warns that Polymestor will suffer punishment for violating hospitality and justice. It helps Hecuba and the Trojan women by considering an attack on the tents, later rebukes Polymestor's abuse of all women, and recognizes that his punishment follows his wrongdoing.

l: Trojan women, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, POLYMESTOR, HECUBA, CHORUS.
s: The Trojan women help Hecuba lure Polymestor into the tent, kill his children, and blind him. They then flee from his pursuit and later prepare to return to their masters' tents.

l: Polymestor's children, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, POLYMESTOR, HECUBA, CHORUS.
s: Polymestor's children accompany him into the tent. The Trojan women stab and kill them while pretending to admire and caress them.

l: Greeks, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, POLYMESTOR, HECUBA, CHORUS.
s: The Greeks are described as friendly toward Polymestor, and their army has conquered Troy. Agamemnon says that Greeks abhor the killing of guests, and the Greeks prepare to sail home.

l: Thracians, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, POLYMESTOR, HECUBA, CHORUS.
s: The Thracians are described as a warlike, spear-brandishing nation that rides horses and is ruled by Mars. Polymestor appeals to the Thracian nation while suffering his punishment.

l: Troy, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, POLYMESTOR, HECUBA, CHORUS.
s: Troy has fallen beneath the Grecian spear, and its towers and city are no longer prosperous. Polydore was sent from Troy to Polymestor, and treasures from Troy are said to be hidden in the tents.

l: Thrace, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, POLYMESTOR, HECUBA, CHORUS.
s: Polymestor says that he was protecting Thrace and its neighboring lands when he killed Polydore, fearing that the Greeks might renew their attack. His territories in Thrace are also mentioned as the place from which he came.

l: Polydore's gold, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, POLYMESTOR, HECUBA, CHORUS.
s: Polydore's gold was brought from Troy and is said by Polymestor to be safe and guarded in his house. Hecuba argues that Polymestor killed Polydore to possess the gold, which he still keeps.

l: murder of Polydore, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, POLYMESTOR, HECUBA, CHORUS.
s: Polymestor murdered Polydore after receiving him from Priam and Hecuba. He claims that the murder was intended to prevent the Greeks from discovering a surviving son of Priam, while Hecuba argues that greed for the gold caused it.

l: murder of Polymestor's children, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, POLYMESTOR, HECUBA, CHORUS.
s: Hecuba and the Trojan women murder Polymestor's children after luring him into the tent. They first approach the children with apparent kindness and then stab them.

l: blinding of Polymestor, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, POLYMESTOR, HECUBA, CHORUS.
s: The Trojan women blind Polymestor by piercing and goring his eyes with their clasps. He emerges from the tent sightless, searches for the women, and asks Agamemnon for help.

l: Hecuba's revenge, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, POLYMESTOR, HECUBA, CHORUS.
s: Hecuba's vengeance consists of the murder of Polymestor's children and the blinding of Polymestor. She tells him that he will never regain his sight or see his children alive, and she rejoices that she has avenged herself.

l: Agamemnon's judgment, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, POLYMESTOR, HECUBA, CHORUS.
s: Agamemnon hears both Polymestor's defense and Hecuba's accusation. He judges that Polymestor killed his guest for the gold and orders him removed rather than allowing him to attack Hecuba.

l: hospitality and its laws, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, POLYMESTOR, HECUBA, CHORUS.
s: The Chorus says that violating hospitality and justice brings destructive punishment. Hecuba and Agamemnon argue that Polymestor acted impiously and unjustly by killing a guest whom he was supposed to protect.

l: The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, notes
s: The unit consists of notes on Euripides’ Hecuba, including textual readings, translations, grammar, and mythological references. It discusses Hecuba’s parentage, her physical dependence in old age, and several passages involving Polymestor, Agamemnon, and the Chorus. Polymestor is described as having committed both injustice and impiety by murdering and leaving his victim unburied. The notes also identify Cynosema as Hecuba’s burial place and mention a naval battle fought there.

l: Hecuba, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, notes
s: The notes state that Homer makes Dymas, rather than Cisseus, the father of Hecuba, while Euripides follows the account naming Cisseus. They also explain passages describing Hecuba’s dependence on attendants and her eventual burial at Cynosema.

l: Euripides, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, notes
s: Euripides is the author whose Hecuba is being annotated. The notes discuss his use of δορυ, κεκλημαι, λιμνη, and other Greek expressions, and propose several textual readings for passages in Hecuba.

l: Polymestor, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, notes
s: Polymestor is described as guilty of both injustice and impiety: he violated human laws and profaned the deity of Jupiter Hospitalis. The notes say that Agamemnon indicates he is to receive punishment on both accounts.

l: Agamemnon, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, notes
s: Agamemnon is presented as wanting to give Polymestor punishment because Polymestor committed an offense against the gods and against justice.

l: Cynosema, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, notes
s: Cynosema is identified as the place of Hecuba’s burial, a promontory of the Thracian Chersonese. The notes also state that the Athenians won a naval victory there over the Peloponnesians and Syracusans during the Peloponnesian war.

l: The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, ORESTES.
s: Electra describes the cursed history of the Tantalids, the killing of Agamemnon by Clytæmnestra, and Orestes' subsequent murder of his mother at Apollo's command. Orestes has been afflicted with madness, weakened by hunger and illness, and persecuted by the Eumenides while Electra cares for him. Argos has decreed that Orestes and Electra must be excluded, and that the Argives will decide whether Orestes should die, but Electra hopes that Menelaus's return from Troy will bring help. Helen sends Hermione to offer libations at Clytæmnestra's tomb, and Menelaus then arrives at the palace.

l: Orestes, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, ORESTES.
s: Orestes killed Clytæmnestra after Apollo commanded him to do so, with Electra and Pylades sharing in the deed. He has since been afflicted with madness, weakness, sleeplessness, hunger, and terror at visions of the Eumenides; Electra watches over and comforts him.

l: Electra, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, ORESTES.
s: Electra remains unmarried and devotes herself to caring for Orestes, guarding his sleep and tending his body. She condemns Apollo for commanding the murder of Clytæmnestra and hopes that Menelaus will aid her and Orestes.

l: Helen, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, ORESTES.
s: Helen has returned from Troy with Menelaus but was sent to the palace by night because she fears the Argives and the fathers of those who died at Ilium. She asks Electra to arrange offerings at Clytæmnestra's tomb and sends Hermione to carry them.

l: Menelaus, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, ORESTES.
s: Menelaus has returned from Troy after long wanderings and has moored his fleet in the Nauplian harbor. He sent Helen ahead to the palace and arrives while Orestes and Electra hope that he will provide assistance.

l: Apollo, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, ORESTES.
s: Apollo commanded Orestes to kill Clytæmnestra, and Orestes says that Apollo offered consolation in words but not relief from the consequences. Apollo also gave Orestes a horn bow and said that it would repel the Furies. Apollo's oracle at the tripod of Themis led Orestes to commit the murder of his mother. Electra and the chorus question the justice of the command because it has brought madness and suffering.

l: Agamemnon, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, ORESTES.
s: Agamemnon was the husband of Clytæmnestra and the father of Electra, Orestes, Chrysothemis, and Iphigenia. Clytæmnestra killed him, and Orestes later killed her.

l: Clytemnestra, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, ORESTES.
s: Clytæmnestra killed Agamemnon after covering him with an inextricable robe. Orestes killed her at Apollo's command, and Helen sends offerings to her tomb.

l: Furies, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, ORESTES.
s: The Eumenides persecute Orestes after the murder of Clytæmnestra, appearing to him as terrifying, snake-haired or Gorgon-visaged beings. The chorus calls them dark, winged goddesses who execute vengeance and slaughter.

l: Chorus, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, ORESTES.
s: The Argive women form the chorus and come to inquire about Orestes' calamity. They approach quietly so as not to disturb his sleep, lament his suffering, and describe the destructive power of the Eumenides.

l: Argives, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, ORESTES.
s: The Argives have decreed that no one may receive Orestes and Electra under a roof or at a hearth, or speak to them. They are to decide whether Orestes should be stoned or killed by the sword, and Helen fears their hostility.

l: the Gods, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, ORESTES.
s: The gods are associated with the calamities afflicting the house of Agamemnon and with the punishment that follows Orestes' deed. The text presents prosperity as unstable and subject to divine destruction.

l: Argos, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, ORESTES.
s: Argos has excluded Orestes and Electra after the murder of Clytæmnestra. The city is preparing to pronounce judgment on whether Orestes should die.

l: Troy, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, ORESTES.
s: Troy is the place from which Menelaus and Helen have returned after the war. Helen's return is feared because many Argives lost their children at Ilium.

l: Agamemnon's palace, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, ORESTES.
s: The action begins before the palace of Agamemnon, where Orestes lies sick on a couch and Electra watches over him. Helen is inside the palace, and Hermione is sent from it to carry offerings to Clytæmnestra's tomb.

l: Orestes' madness, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, ORESTES.
s: Orestes' madness causes him to lose his memory, become violently agitated, and see the Eumenides as attacking figures. His fits alternate with periods of sleep, weakness, grief, and restored awareness.

l: Clytæmnestra's murder, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, ORESTES.
s: Orestes committed the murder of Clytæmnestra because Apollo commanded it, while Electra and Pylades also took part. The deed has brought Orestes madness, public condemnation, and the threat of execution.

l: trial of Orestes and Electra, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, ORESTES.
s: The Argives are to decide whether Orestes should be stoned or killed with a sword. Orestes and Electra hope that Menelaus, as Agamemnon's brother, will help them before the decision is made.

l: Menelaus's return from Troy, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, ORESTES.
s: Menelaus's return from Troy gives Electra hope of assistance for herself and Orestes. He has brought Helen back, sent her to the palace by night, and now arrives with his fleet at the Nauplian harbor.

l: death, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, ORESTES.
s: Death is presented as the expected outcome for Orestes because he cannot eat and has been condemned by the city. Electra says that she will choose to live or die with him.

l: the oracle of Apollo, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, ORESTES.
s: The oracle of Apollo commanded Orestes to kill his mother. Orestes later blames Apollo because the oracle led him to an impious act while providing only verbal consolation for its consequences.

l: madness and divine punishment, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, ORESTES.
s: After killing Clytæmnestra, Orestes is punished by madness and pursued by the Eumenides. His condition includes terror, hallucinations, physical weakness, fasting, and repeated loss of reason.

l: family curse of the Tantalids, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, ORESTES.
s: The history of the Tantalids is presented as a succession of divine and familial crimes, beginning with Tantalus and continuing through Pelops, Atreus, Thyestes, Agamemnon, Clytæmnestra, and Orestes. The chorus treats this lineage as marked by recurring slaughter, grief, and unstable prosperity.

l: The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, MENELAUS, ORESTES, CHORUS.
s: Menelaus returns from Troy and finds Orestes living in extreme misery after killing his mother, Clytæmnestra, in revenge for Agamemnon's death. Tyndarus condemns Orestes and urges Menelaus not to save him, arguing that Orestes violated Greek law by committing matricide instead of pursuing a legal charge or accepting banishment. Orestes defends himself by claiming that Apollo commanded the killing and that he acted to avenge Agamemnon, while asking Menelaus to repay Agamemnon's aid by saving him and Electra. Menelaus promises to seek help through persuasion, but Orestes believes he has been betrayed when Menelaus leaves, and Pylades arrives from Phocis.

l: Menelaus, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, MENELAUS, ORESTES, CHORUS.
s: Menelaus returns from Troy and learns that Orestes is suffering from madness and persecution after killing Clytæmnestra. He expresses willingness to help Orestes but says he lacks sufficient allies to oppose Argos by force, so he will try to persuade Tyndarus and the city.

l: Orestes, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, MENELAUS, ORESTES, CHORUS.
s: Orestes identifies himself to Menelaus as Agamemnon's son and describes his disordered body, madness, visions, social exclusion, and impending sentence to death by stoning. He defends killing Clytæmnestra as vengeance for Agamemnon and appeals to Menelaus to save his life and Electra's.

l: Tyndarus, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, MENELAUS, ORESTES, CHORUS.
s: Tyndarus arrives mourning Clytæmnestra and condemns Orestes as an unholy matricide. He argues that Orestes should have brought a legal charge against Clytæmnestra or accepted banishment, and he plans to urge the Argives to sentence Orestes and Electra to death.

l: Agamemnon, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, MENELAUS, ORESTES, CHORUS.
s: Agamemnon is described as having led the Greeks to Troy and as having been killed by Clytæmnestra after returning from war. Orestes says that Agamemnon's kindness and his sacrifice for Menelaus should move Menelaus to protect Agamemnon's children.

l: Clytemnestra, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, MENELAUS, ORESTES, CHORUS.
s: Clytæmnestra killed Agamemnon and secretly took Ægisthus as her husband. Orestes killed her in retaliation, while Tyndarus condemns both her murder of Agamemnon and Orestes' response.

l: Pylades, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, MENELAUS, ORESTES, CHORUS.
s: Pylades helped Orestes carry out the vengeance and death of Clytæmnestra. Orestes calls him a faithful friend in adversity, and he arrives from Phocis at the end of the unit.

l: Helen, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, MENELAUS, ORESTES, CHORUS.
s: Helen is identified as Menelaus's wife and as the reason Menelaus went to Troy. Tyndarus calls her perfidious and says he does not commend Menelaus for going to war on her account.

l: Aegisthus, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, MENELAUS, ORESTES, CHORUS.
s: Ægisthus was Clytæmnestra's secret husband in Agamemnon's palace. Orestes says that he killed Ægisthus before killing Clytæmnestra.

l: Apollo, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, MENELAUS, ORESTES, CHORUS.
s: Apollo commanded Orestes to kill Clytæmnestra, according to Orestes. Orestes therefore attributes responsibility for the deed to Apollo and asks how he could escape punishment if the god who commanded him does not deliver him.

l: Hermione, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, MENELAUS, ORESTES, CHORUS.
s: Hermione is Menelaus's daughter. Orestes says that he does not ask Menelaus to kill her and asks him to preserve her life along with his own and Electra's.

l: Furies, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, MENELAUS, ORESTES, CHORUS.
s: The Furies pursue Orestes in revenge for Clytæmnestra's blood. Orestes sees three virgins resembling night and says that the Furies would also have pursued him had he failed to avenge Agamemnon.

l: the Gods, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, MENELAUS, ORESTES, CHORUS.
s: The Gods are invoked as the powers involved in Orestes' command, suffering, and possible rescue. Menelaus says that the Gods hate excessive vehemence, while Orestes argues that people are servants of the Gods whatever those Gods may be.

l: Chorus, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, MENELAUS, ORESTES, CHORUS.
s: The Chorus observes Tyndarus approaching in mourning and comments on the misery of families marked by notorious calamities. It also joins Orestes in asking Menelaus to help those in need.

l: Argives, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, MENELAUS, ORESTES, CHORUS.
s: The Argives have rejected Orestes and do not allow him to live among them. They are expected to decide his fate that very day, with death by stoning presented as the sentence.

l: Greeks, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, MENELAUS, ORESTES, CHORUS.
s: The Greeks are described as having been gathered by Agamemnon for the expedition to Troy. Orestes claims that his actions may help all Greece by deterring women from murdering their husbands.

l: Troy, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, MENELAUS, ORESTES, CHORUS.
s: Troy is the place from which Menelaus has returned after the war. Agamemnon's expedition there is presented as having arisen from the wrong done by Helen.

l: Argos, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, MENELAUS, ORESTES, CHORUS.
s: Argos is the city whose citizens reject Orestes and threaten to stone him. Menelaus says that he cannot defeat Argos by force because he has arrived with only one spear and few allies.

l: Agamemnon's palace, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, MENELAUS, ORESTES, CHORUS.
s: Agamemnon's palace is described as a house surrounded by lamentable woes. It was the place where Clytæmnestra killed Agamemnon and where Ægisthus became her secret husband.

l: Agamemnon’s murder, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, MENELAUS, ORESTES, CHORUS.
s: Agamemnon's death was reported to Menelaus by Glaucus while Menelaus was landing his ships at Malea. He was killed by Clytæmnestra in the bath after returning from Troy.

l: Clytæmnestra's murder, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, MENELAUS, ORESTES, CHORUS.
s: Clytæmnestra's murder was committed by Orestes with Pylades after Orestes had killed Ægisthus. Orestes calls the act unholy but maintains that it avenged Agamemnon and was commanded by Apollo.

l: the Trojan War, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, MENELAUS, ORESTES, CHORUS.
s: The Trojan War caused Menelaus and Agamemnon to be absent from the palace for many years. Tyndarus connects Agamemnon's death and the resulting hostility toward his family with the events at Troy.

l: Orestes' trial and sentence, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, MENELAUS, ORESTES, CHORUS.
s: Orestes says that the city will decide his case that day. He expects the Argives to sentence him to death by stoning, while Tyndarus plans to encourage the assembled multitude to impose that sentence on Orestes and Electra.

l: matricide, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, MENELAUS, ORESTES, CHORUS.
s: Orestes acknowledges that he committed matricide by killing Clytæmnestra. He argues that the act was necessary to avenge Agamemnon, while Tyndarus calls it a greater wickedness than Clytæmnestra's crime.

l: blood pollution, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, MENELAUS, ORESTES, CHORUS.
s: Orestes cannot wash the blood from his hands because he is excluded from every house. Tyndarus says that earlier law required a person guilty of murder to atone through banishment and prevented others from killing him in return.

l: divine command and responsibility, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, MENELAUS, ORESTES, CHORUS.
s: Orestes says that Apollo commanded him to kill Clytæmnestra and therefore claims that Apollo, rather than he alone, bears responsibility for the deed. He argues that the god's command should provide a means of removing his pollution and saving him from death.

l: Justice, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, MENELAUS, ORESTES, CHORUS.
s: Tyndarus argues that justice required Orestes to bring a formal charge against Clytæmnestra or remove her from the house rather than kill her. Orestes answers that he acted to avenge Agamemnon and prevent women from treating the murder of their husbands as permissible, while Menelaus says that necessity must be considered by the wise.

l: The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, PYLADES, ORESTES, CHORUS.
s: Pylades joins Orestes and learns that Menelaus has refused to save Orestes and Electra, while Tyndarus has supported their condemnation. Orestes and Electra are tried by the Argive citizens for the murder of Clytemnestra and sentenced to die, though Orestes persuades the assembly to let them avoid stoning by promising self-slaughter. A Messenger reports the arguments made at the Argive assembly and describes Pylades supporting Orestes. The Chorus and Electra lament the madness, inherited violence, and declining fortune of the house of Pelops.

l: Orestes, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, PYLADES, ORESTES, CHORUS.
s: Orestes is guarded in the palace and faces trial by the Argive citizens for killing his mother. He explains that he acted to avenge Agamemnon, but the assembly condemns him and Electra to die. He suffers from heaven-inflicted madness and plans to die by self-slaughter with Electra, while Pylades supports and guides him.

l: Pylades, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, PYLADES, ORESTES, CHORUS.
s: Pylades comes quickly to warn Orestes and Electra about the council assembled against them. Though Strophius has exiled him for sharing in Clytemnestra's murder, he remains devoted to Orestes, supports him through his illness, and conducts him from the assembly.

l: Electra, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, PYLADES, ORESTES, CHORUS.
s: Electra remains in the palace under guard and is condemned to die with Orestes for the murder of Clytemnestra. She learns of the assembly's decision from the Messenger and laments the ruin of her family and the approaching self-slaughter.

l: Chorus, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, PYLADES, ORESTES, CHORUS.
s: The Chorus describes the inherited calamities of the house of Atreus and condemns both the murder of a mother and the wickedness surrounding it. It laments Orestes' madness, Electra's suffering, and the destruction of the descendants of Pelops.

l: Menelaus, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, PYLADES, ORESTES, CHORUS.
s: Menelaus comes to the land but refuses Orestes' request to prevent the citizens from killing him and Electra. Orestes and Pylades regard his conduct as basely hostile to his friends.

l: Helen, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, PYLADES, ORESTES, CHORUS.
s: She is in the palace of Orestes after arriving with Menelaus. Orestes and Pylades describe her as the woman who destroyed many of the Greeks, and Pylades says that Menelaus was brought there by her.

l: Tyndarus, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, PYLADES, ORESTES, CHORUS.
s: He is present and argues against Orestes because Orestes killed his daughter. He favors the ties connecting him with Clytemnestra over those connecting him with Orestes' father and privately encourages speeches seeking their death.

l: Agamemnon, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, PYLADES, ORESTES, CHORUS.
s: Agamemnon is Orestes' father, whose death Orestes avenges by killing Clytemnestra. The Messenger says that one speaker proposed honoring Orestes because he defended Agamemnon's household and memory.

l: Clytemnestra, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, PYLADES, ORESTES, CHORUS.
s: Clytemnestra is the mother whom Orestes killed in retaliation for Agamemnon's death. The Chorus recalls her warning Orestes against the deed, while the assembly debates whether her killing was justified.

l: Messenger, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, PYLADES, ORESTES, CHORUS.
s: The Messenger reports the decision of the Argive assembly to Electra. He recounts the speeches for and against Orestes, explains that both Orestes and Electra were condemned, and describes Pylades leading Orestes away in grief.

l: Argives, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, PYLADES, ORESTES, CHORUS.
s: The Argive citizens surround the palace with guards and decide the fate of Orestes and Electra. Their assembly condemns them to death, though the Messenger reports that some citizens favored banishment or argued in Orestes' defense.

l: Argive assembly, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, PYLADES, ORESTES, CHORUS.
s: The Argive assembly gathers at the place where Danaus first collected the people. It hears competing speeches about Orestes' deed and votes that Orestes and Electra must die.

l: friends and companions, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, PYLADES, ORESTES, CHORUS.
s: Friends and companions are presented as sharing one another's troubles. Pylades is praised as a friend more valuable than numerous relatives, and Orestes' friends accompany him from the assembly while mourning and pitying him.

l: Argos, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, PYLADES, ORESTES, CHORUS.
s: Argos is the city where Orestes and Electra are watched, tried, and condemned. Its people are portrayed as capable of good deliberation under good leaders but dangerous when led by evil or intemperate speakers.

l: Greece, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, PYLADES, ORESTES, CHORUS.
s: Greece is invoked in the lament for the lost happiness and valor of the descendants of Atreus. Electra addresses the land of Greece while mourning the destruction of her family.

l: palace of Orestes, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, PYLADES, ORESTES, CHORUS.
s: The palace is where Orestes and Electra are confined under guard and where Helen is staying. Pylades urges Orestes to leave it before the Argive decree is carried out.

l: Agamemnon's tomb, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, PYLADES, ORESTES, CHORUS.
s: Orestes intends to go to his father's tomb to supplicate Agamemnon for protection. Pylades agrees that this appeal is just and offers to guide him there.

l: council of state, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, PYLADES, ORESTES, CHORUS.
s: The council of state assembles against Orestes and Electra and appears ready to kill them. Pylades comes after hearing of it and seeing the city prepared against them.

l: trial of Orestes and Electra, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, PYLADES, ORESTES, CHORUS.
s: The trial concerns whether Orestes and Electra should live or die for the murder committed against Clytemnestra. The Argive assembly hears several speeches and finally condemns both of them.

l: Clytæmnestra's murder, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, PYLADES, ORESTES, CHORUS.
s: The murder of Clytemnestra is the charge brought against Orestes and Electra. Orestes defends it as revenge for Agamemnon, but the Chorus presents it as a deed that brings madness, grief, and continuing bloodshed.

l: Orestes' trial and sentence, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, PYLADES, ORESTES, CHORUS.
s: The Argive citizens impose a death sentence on Orestes and Electra. Orestes avoids being immediately stoned by promising that he and Electra will end their lives that day.

l: self-slaughter of Orestes and Electra, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, PYLADES, ORESTES, CHORUS.
s: Orestes promises the assembly that he will quit life by self-slaughter together with Electra. Pylades leads him away as their friends mourn, while Electra prepares for the same fate.

l: family curse of the Tantalids, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, PYLADES, ORESTES, CHORUS.
s: The Chorus traces the present catastrophe to the ancient calamities of the house of Atreus, including the golden lamb, Thyestes' feast, and successive murders. It presents the family as repeatedly suffering bloodshed in response to bloodshed.

l: murder and revenge, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, PYLADES, ORESTES, CHORUS.
s: Murder and revenge govern the history of the family, with Orestes killing Clytemnestra in revenge for Agamemnon. The Chorus questions the justice of the deed while recognizing the continuing chain of violence.

l: Orestes' madness, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, PYLADES, ORESTES, CHORUS.
s: Orestes is described as overcome by heaven-inflicted madness and as a prey to the Eumenides. He fears that the goddesses may stop him, and Pylades takes responsibility for assisting him despite the danger.

l: sword, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, PYLADES, ORESTES, CHORUS.
s: The sword is one of the possible means by which Electra asks whether she and Orestes must die. The Chorus also recalls Orestes brandishing a blood-stained sword after killing his mother.

l: the noose, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, PYLADES, ORESTES, CHORUS.
s: The noose is proposed by the Messenger as another means by which Electra and Orestes may end their lives. He tells Electra to prepare either the sword or the noose.

l: house of Pelops, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, PYLADES, ORESTES, CHORUS.
s: The house of Pelops is presented as having lost its entire line and former happiness. Electra traces its ruin through the crimes of Pelops, the golden lamb, Thyestes' feast, and the marriage of Ærope.

l: death and fortune, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, PYLADES, ORESTES, CHORUS.
s: The Chorus presents human fortune as unstable, uncertain, and subject to sudden reversal. It says that mortals endure different sufferings in turn and that divine envy has seized the former happiness of Orestes' family.

l: The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, ELECTRA, ORESTES, PYLADES, CHORUS.
s: Orestes, Electra, and Pylades, condemned to die, resolve to avenge themselves on Menelaus by murdering Helen and, if necessary, setting the palace on fire. Electra proposes seizing Hermione as a hostage so that Menelaus will spare them, or killing Hermione if he refuses. Helen is attacked inside Orestes' house, while Hermione arrives from Clytemnestra's tomb and is seized at sword point. The Chorus guards the approaches and hears a Phrygian servant emerge from the palace to report what has happened.

l: Orestes, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, ELECTRA, ORESTES, PYLADES, CHORUS.
s: Orestes is condemned to die with Electra and considers killing himself with a sword rather than suffering a disgraceful death. He agrees with Pylades to murder Helen, seize Hermione as a hostage, and take revenge on Menelaus. He recalls that he slew his mother and prays to Agamemnon and Zeus for success.

l: Electra, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, ELECTRA, ORESTES, PYLADES, CHORUS.
s: Electra mourns Orestes and refuses to abandon him, asking to die by his sword rather than be killed by the Argives. She proposes the plan to seize Hermione and use her as a pledge for the safety of herself, Orestes, and Pylades. She guards the house, directs the Chorus, helps conceal the attack on Helen, and orders Hermione to be held at sword point.

l: Pylades, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, ELECTRA, ORESTES, PYLADES, CHORUS.
s: Pylades insists that he cannot live if Orestes dies, because he helped commit and plan the killing of Clytemnestra. He joins Orestes in planning Helen's murder and accepts Electra's plan involving Hermione. He enters the house with Orestes armed with a concealed sword.

l: Helen, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, ELECTRA, ORESTES, PYLADES, CHORUS.
s: Helen is targeted by Orestes and Pylades as revenge for the suffering caused by the Trojan War. She is attacked inside Orestes' house and cries out that she is dying and that Menelaus does not help her. The unit ends while the result of the attack is being reported.

l: Hermione, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, ELECTRA, ORESTES, PYLADES, CHORUS.
s: Hermione comes from Clytemnestra's tomb after pouring libations for her mother. Electra draws her into the house under the pretense of seeking her help and has her seized as a hostage. Orestes advances on her, and Electra orders that a sword be held to her neck.

l: Menelaus, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, ELECTRA, ORESTES, PYLADES, CHORUS.
s: Menelaus is accused of failing to defend Orestes and of valuing his scepter and recovered marriage over his friends. Orestes and Pylades plan to avenge themselves on him by murdering Helen. Electra expects that concern for Hermione may force Menelaus to spare them.

l: Agamemnon, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, ELECTRA, ORESTES, PYLADES, CHORUS.
s: Agamemnon is remembered as Orestes' father and as a ruler of Greece who was not a tyrant. Orestes, Electra, and Pylades call upon him from the realm of the dead to help his children, and Pylades asks him to preserve them.

l: Chorus, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, ELECTRA, ORESTES, PYLADES, CHORUS.
s: The Chorus condemns Helen as an object of hatred among women and blames her for filling Greece with tears. It guards the roads approaching the palace, watches for allies and enemies, and helps maintain the deception surrounding Helen's attack. It hears Helen's cries and awaits news from a Phrygian servant.

l: palace of Orestes, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, ELECTRA, ORESTES, PYLADES, CHORUS.
s: Helen is inside Orestes' house when Orestes and Pylades enter to attack her. The conspirators plan to bolt her attendants out of different parts of the house and threaten to burn the palace if the murder fails. The house becomes the scene of Helen's cries and the seizure of Hermione.

l: the tomb of Clytæmnestra, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, ELECTRA, ORESTES, PYLADES, CHORUS.
s: Hermione goes to Clytemnestra's tomb to pour libations for her mother. Her return from the tomb gives Electra and the others the opportunity to seize her as a hostage.

l: sword, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, ELECTRA, ORESTES, PYLADES, CHORUS.
s: Orestes initially considers using the sword to kill himself, while Electra asks that Orestes kill her rather than let the Argives execute her. Orestes and Pylades conceal swords beneath their robes for the attack on Helen, and a sword is held to Hermione's neck.

l: Clytæmnestra's murder, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, ELECTRA, ORESTES, PYLADES, CHORUS.
s: Orestes says that he slew his mother, while Pylades says that he directed the sword and Electra says that she incited Orestes and freed him from delay. Their participation in the killing is presented as the reason for their present suffering and threatened punishment.

l: the planned murder of Helen, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, ELECTRA, ORESTES, PYLADES, CHORUS.
s: Orestes and Pylades plan to enter the house pretending to lament, conceal their swords, isolate Helen's attendants, and kill Helen. They justify the intended murder as vengeance for the Greeks who died and for the families left bereaved by the Trojan War. The attack begins, and Helen is heard crying that she has been slain.

l: the threatened killing of Hermione, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, ELECTRA, ORESTES, PYLADES, CHORUS.
s: Electra proposes that Orestes hold Hermione as a hostage after Helen's death. If Menelaus threatens Orestes, Electra, or Pylades, they are to threaten Hermione's life; if Menelaus refuses to spare them, Orestes is to plunge the sword into Hermione's neck.

l: Orestes' trial and sentence, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, ELECTRA, ORESTES, PYLADES, CHORUS.
s: The land has decreed that Orestes and Electra die. They believe death is unavoidable unless they can obtain safety through their plot against Helen and their seizure of Hermione.

l: friendship and loyalty, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, ELECTRA, ORESTES, PYLADES, CHORUS.
s: Orestes praises Pylades as a friend more valuable than riches or kingdoms. Pylades refuses to abandon Orestes in misfortune, saying that he shared in the killing of Clytemnestra and must share its consequences. Orestes, Electra, and Pylades describe their friendship as a single bond exposed to one common danger.

l: marriage, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, ELECTRA, ORESTES, PYLADES, CHORUS.
s: Orestes says that he had betrothed Electra to Pylades because he revered their friendship, and he urges Pylades to marry elsewhere and become a father if Orestes dies. Pylades rejects this separation and says that he regards Electra as his wife because he has courted her. Electra later presents Hermione's possible marriage to Pylades as a reason for their hoped-for safety.

l: revenge, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, ELECTRA, ORESTES, PYLADES, CHORUS.
s: Orestes, Electra, and Pylades seek revenge against Menelaus and Helen rather than accepting a slavish death. Their revenge includes the planned murder of Helen, the possible burning of the palace, and the threatened killing of Hermione if Menelaus refuses to spare them.

l: The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, PHRYGIAN, CHORUS.
s: The Phrygian recounts how Orestes and Pylades entered the palace, killed Clytemnestra, and attempted to kill Helen before Helen vanished and the Phrygian attendants fled. Orestes then threatens to kill Hermione and burn the palace unless Menelaus secures a judgment that will save him, Electra, and Pylades. Apollo appears, declares that Helen has been preserved as an immortal daughter of Zeus, and orders that Orestes stand trial at Athens, marry Hermione, and allow Pylades to marry Electra. Apollo also commands Menelaus to let Orestes rule Argos and to return to Sparta.

l: Orestes, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, PHRYGIAN, CHORUS.
s: Orestes enters Helen's chamber with Pylades, kills Clytemnestra, and attempts to kill Helen. He threatens to kill Hermione and burn the palace unless Menelaus helps secure his survival, but Apollo orders him to leave the land for a year, stand trial at Athens for shedding his mother's blood, marry Hermione, and eventually rule Argos.

l: Menelaus, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, PHRYGIAN, CHORUS.
s: Menelaus arrives after hearing of Helen's supposed death and confronts Orestes, demanding the release of Hermione and justice for the murders. Apollo orders him to let Orestes reign over Argos and to return to Sparta, which he has as Helen's dowry.

l: Helen, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, PHRYGIAN, CHORUS.
s: Helen is attacked by Orestes and Pylades but vanishes from the palace before they can kill her. Apollo reveals that he preserved her at Zeus's command and that she now dwells immortally among the stars with Castor and Pollux.

l: Pylades, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, PHRYGIAN, CHORUS.
s: Pylades assists Orestes in the attack on Clytemnestra and Helen and fights the Phrygian attendants. He helps Orestes threaten the palace and Hermione, and Apollo approves his marriage to Electra.

l: Electra, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, PHRYGIAN, CHORUS.
s: Electra is among those threatened with death if Menelaus brings aid against Orestes. Orestes orders her to set fire to the palace, and Apollo declares that she is to marry Pylades.

l: Hermione, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, PHRYGIAN, CHORUS.
s: Hermione arrives at the palace as Clytemnestra falls and is seized by Orestes and Pylades. Orestes threatens to kill her, but Apollo declares that she is destined to marry Orestes.

l: Phrygian, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, PHRYGIAN, CHORUS.
s: The Phrygian attendant escapes the palace and recounts how Orestes and Pylades attacked Helen and killed Clytemnestra. He fears death but is pardoned by Orestes after declaring that every person, even a slave, prefers to see the light.

l: Apollo, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, PHRYGIAN, CHORUS.
s: Apollo intervenes to stop the conflict and explains that Helen was preserved and made immortal. He orders Orestes to undergo trial at Athens, assigns the marriages of Orestes to Hermione and Pylades to Electra, and commands Menelaus and Orestes to end their quarrel.

l: Argives, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, PHRYGIAN, CHORUS.
s: The Argives are expected to respond if they hear the noise at the palace. Menelaus calls on them to come armed to his aid, while Orestes tells Menelaus to persuade the city not to condemn him and his companions.

l: Greeks, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, PHRYGIAN, CHORUS.
s: The Greeks are said to have suffered deaths in the conflict with Troy because the Gods used the war to reduce the excessive pride and population of mortals. Helen's beauty is presented as the cause of the Greeks' and Phrygians' destruction.

l: Phrygians, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, PHRYGIAN, CHORUS.
s: The Phrygians serving in the palace try to come to Helen's assistance after Orestes attacks her. They fight Pylades but are defeated by the Greek force, with some fleeing, some being wounded, and some dying.

l: Furies, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, PHRYGIAN, CHORUS.
s: The Furies are said to have driven the house of the Atridae toward repeated bloodshed. Apollo declares that Orestes must face the charge imposed by the three Furies at the hill of Mars.

l: Argos, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, PHRYGIAN, CHORUS.
s: Argos is the land in which Orestes claims the right to live and rule. Apollo orders Menelaus to allow Orestes to reign there.

l: Troy, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, PHRYGIAN, CHORUS.
s: Troy is described as the place from which Menelaus has returned after enduring many hardships. The conflict surrounding Troy is connected with the deaths caused by Helen's beauty and the Gods' purposes.

l: Phrygia, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, PHRYGIAN, CHORUS.
s: Phrygia is represented through the Phrygian attendants and the destroyed city of Ilion. The Phrygian narrator laments the ruin of his country and the defeat of its people by the Greeks.

l: Agamemnon's palace, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, PHRYGIAN, CHORUS.
s: The palace becomes the scene of Clytemnestra's murder, Helen's disappearance, the fighting between the Greek attackers and Phrygian attendants, and Orestes' threat to burn the building. Orestes and his companions occupy its battlements while Menelaus confronts them outside.

l: sword, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, PHRYGIAN, CHORUS.
s: Orestes and Pylades use drawn swords in the attack on Helen and Clytemnestra. Orestes later holds a sword over Hermione's neck, and Apollo's intervention causes him to release her.

l: the Trojan War, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, PHRYGIAN, CHORUS.
s: The war is represented as the conflict in which Greeks and Phrygians suffered mass deaths because of Helen. Apollo says that the Gods brought Greeks and Trojans together to humble mortals whose numbers and pride had become excessive.

l: the planned murder of Helen, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, PHRYGIAN, CHORUS.
s: Orestes attempts to kill Helen, but she vanishes from the palace before the sword reaches her. Apollo states that Helen was not slain and that he carried her away to become immortal.
